title: Recordanelles for transcriptome-wide single-cell RNA recording in human cells - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractTranscriptomic measurement technologies provide powerful approaches to understand biology but are limited to providing either a high-resolution snapshot at a moment in time or a low-resolution history of transcription constrained to a few genes over a narrow time range. Here, we introduce the ‘recordanelle’, a single-component synthetic organelle capable of recording the transcriptome in human cells. Recordanelles are composed of a mitochondrial membrane anchor, a condensate assembler and a poly(A)-binding protein. We demonstrate that the recordanelle can be engineered to recruit engineered RNAs or a sampling of up to 90% of all endogenous mRNAs and protect them over several days. We further show that transient and dynamic transcriptional responses resulting from inducible promoters or interferon signaling are preserved throughout time within the recordanelle at the single-cell level. This work provides a nondisruptive and unbiased transcriptome-wide single-cell RNA recording technology to enable a deeper understanding of biology.

MainCells orchestrate development and adapt to intracellular and extracellular cues by dynamically regulating gene transcription. However, most current approaches to measure transcription are disruptive and capture only static snapshots1. Metabolic or enzymatic labeling of nascent or tagged RNAs can add temporal resolution to transcriptomics but these approaches are constrained by a lack of continuous transcriptome sampling, indirect inference of transcriptional activity, substantial input requirements or limited scalability beyond a small number of RNA species2,3,4,5,6,7. DNA-based molecular recording methods that encode transient information into DNA enable retrospective reconstruction of gene expression events, yet have been largely confined to prokaryotes and/or a small set of target genes8,9. Overcoming these limitations requires approaches for nondisruptive, unbiased, transcriptome-wide recording in eukaryotic cells.The ideal RNA recording system would recruit, protect and accommodate a representative sampling of the transcriptome within a storage archive throughout time and cell division without bias or altering cellular physiology. We conceived of a solution meeting these demands, which we term ‘recordanelle’ (RNA recording organelle)—a genetically encoded system that is inspired by the principles of biomolecular condensation10,11,12 to drive the unbiased and scalable storage of endogenous cytoplasmic RNAs within an orthogonal and heritable organelle (Fig. 1). The recordanelle is created with a single protein harboring three components—a generic RNA-binding domain (RBD), a biomolecular condensate assembler domain and a mitochondrial membrane anchor. Together, the RBD and the assembler domain collect endogenous RNAs in a protective environment, which is stabilized by the mitochondrial membrane anchor at an easily isolatable structure through time and cell division (Supplementary Notes). While transiently expressed RNAs are lost in normal cells, they should be preserved within the recordanelles of engineered cells. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) would then allow reconstruction of the gene expression history of recordanelle-containing cells.Fig. 1: Recording transient gene expression events.Full size imagea, In a cell continuously expressing a set of genes A (gray), a stimulus triggers a transient expression of a set of genes B (magenta). Once the stimulus has passed, genes B progressively decay. When these cells are sampled and their RNA content is analyzed at different time points, the set of genes A can always be detected but expression of genes B can only be detected at t2, after the stimulation and before they decay to baseline. b, In cells expressing an RNA recording organelle (recordanelle) mounted onto the mitochondria, once genes B are expressed upon stimulation, they are captured within the organelle, where they are protected from decay. The RNA content of the entire cell can then be analyzed at a later time point t3, at which the recorded transcripts remain detectable. To improve the signal-to-noise ratio, recordanelles can be purified by mitochondrial extraction, enriching for the captured and recorded transcripts.Here, we confirm that mitochondrial-anchored recordanelles constructed with the phage-derived RBDs ms2 bacteriophage major capsid protein (MCP) or pp7 coat protein (PCP) efficiently recruit engineered RNAs harboring their targeted stem loops ms2 or pp7, respectively. Swapping out the sequence-specific phage RBDs for mRNA-binding domains demonstrates transcriptome-wide recruitment, faithful purification by fractionation and deep-sequencing-based transcriptome reconstruction. Lastly, we show that the best-performing recordanelle—recordanelleV2 containing TOM201–70 as the mitochondrial membrane anchor, TAF15N as the assembler peptide and PABPC4∆C161A as the mRNA-binding domain—records transient and dynamic transcriptional responses resulting from synthetic inducers or interferon (IFN) signaling in bulk samples and in single cells. Critically, these transient transcriptional responses cannot be observed in nonengineered cells and recordanelle expression and transcriptome recording over several days does not alter mitochondrial function or cellular physiology.ResultsRBDs efficiently capture selected RNAs within recordanellesToward creating the recordanelle, we determined whether we could recruit specific RNAs within mitochondrial membrane-anchored biomolecular condensates without disrupting the transcriptome (Fig. 2a). For the RBD part of the recordanelle, we used MCP and PCP, which specifically bind ms2 and pp7 stem loops, respectively13,14. For mitochondrial anchoring, we used the first 70 aa of the human mitochondrial protein TOM20, which has been described previously15,16. For the assembler protein, we decided to test several intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins that have been previously used to engineer synthetic condensates (DDX4C, EWSR1N, FUSN, hnRNPA1C, TAF15N and TDP43C)17,18,19, as well as two full-length members of the FET family (FUS and EWSR1)20,21,22, several IDR variants of FUS with distinct condensation behaviors21,23, several IDR1 and NTF2 variants of the core stress granule protein G3BP1 (refs. 24,25,26) and the protein UBQL2, which has been shown to form condensates immiscible with other cellular condensates27 (Supplementary Notes). As controls, we created recordanelle constructs without an assembler (∆AP) or RBD.Fig. 2: Specific RNA recruitment in recordanelles.Full size imagea, A recordanelle is formed by a mitochondrial anchor (MA; such as the first 70 aa of TOM20), which tethers the organelle to the outer mitochondrial membrane, an assembler peptide (AP), inspired by phase separation principles, and an RBD. When cells are cotransfected with constructs encoding ms2-tagged and pp7-tagged RNAs, as well as a recordanelle containing MCP as the RBD, the ms2-tagged mRNA is specifically localized within the organelle. When the RBD is exchanged by PCP, the pp7-tagged RNA is recruited there. b, FISH of HEK293T cells expressing MA::FUSQG::MCP or MA::FUSQG::PCP reveals specific recruitment of either mCherry::ms2 (by MCP) or mCherry::pp7 (by PCP) mRNAs to the recordanelles. mCherry protein, blue; apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF; mitochondrial marker), yellow; recordanelle (HA), magenta; mCherry mRNA, cyan. Scale bars, 20 µm. c, Specific RNA recruitment analysis by qPCR in the mitochondrial fraction for cells cotransfected with dual reporter (mCherry::ms2•EGFP::pp7) and recordanelles containing the MA, different APs fused to MCP, PCP or no RBD. Relative gene expression for mCherry, EGFP and YWHAZ was calculated using the 2−∆∆Ct method with MT-ATP6 as the reference gene and mock transfection as the control sample. The heat map shows the mean of at least three independent experiments per condition. The selectivity is calculated as the log10 ratio of mCherry expression to EGFP expression; positive values indicate mCherry:ms2 enrichment, whereas negative values indicate EGFP::pp7 enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 2a). d, Differential gene expression analysis by RNA-seq of full cell RNA sample or RNA extracted from the mitochondrial fraction for HEK293T cells cotransfected with dual reporter and recordanelles containing FUSQG as AP fused to MCP, PCP or no RBD. Left, differential expression for MA::FUSQG::MCP versus MA::FUSQG. Right, differential expression for MA::FUSQG::PCP versus MA::FUSQG. Significantly enriched genes are shown in magenta and significantly depleted genes are shown in blue. Dashed lines indicate thresholds for significance at a |log2FC| of 1.5 and FDR of 0.01.To characterize the localization of recordanelles and target RNAs, we performed transient transfection experiments in HEK293T cells containing a reporter construct expressing mCherry fused to either ms2 (mCherry::ms2) or pp7 (mCherry::pp7) stem loops (Fig. 2a). Using immunofluorescence (IF) and RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), we found that the recordanelles faithfully localize to the mitochondrial surface and specifically recruit the target RNAs (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Video 1). For instance, using FISH probes targeting the mCherry sequence, we observed a strong enrichment of mCherry::ms2 RNA in MCP-containing but not PCP-containing recordanelles. Swapping mCherry::ms2 for mCherry::pp7 led to mCherry RNA localization exclusively within PCP-containing recordanelles. This demonstrates efficient and specific recruitment of engineered RNAs within recordanelles inside living cells.To quantify RNA enrichment efficiency across recordanelles, we transiently transfected HEK293T cells with a dual reporter, as well as constructs containing a fixed MCP as the RBD and TOM201–70 as the anchor but with varying assemblers. The dual-reporter construct expressed mCherry and EGFP fused to ms2 (mCherry::ms2) and pp7 (EGFP::pp7) stem loops, respectively, enabling the precise quantification of targeted RNAs within the recordanelle compared to a nonspecific RNA expressed from the same construct. Using cellular fractionation and qPCR, we observed an enrichment of mCherry::ms2 RNAs within the recordanelles (that is, mitochondrial cell fraction) with an efficiency ranging from 3-fold to 11-fold compared to a mock control (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2a). We also observed enrichment of target RNAs when using a ∆AP control construct. Some recordanelle architectures (for example, FUSQG and FUSN), however, seem to exhibit a higher mean mCherry::ms2 enrichment (not statistically significant). On the basis of this small-scale screen, we selected several lead candidates for subsequent analysis (FUSQG, FUSN, EWSR1 and TAF15N).We also observed nonspecific enrichment of EGFP::pp7 or the endogenous housekeeping mRNA YWHAZ when using a subset of constructs (for example, FUS6D and G3BP1), which could arise because of nonspecific RNA binding through the intrinsic RBDs of certain assemblers. Consequently, we additionally assessed the selectivity of the MCP-based recordanelles by calculating the ratio of mCherry::ms2 to EGFP::pp7 mRNAs and found values ranging from 1.2-fold to 6-fold. We found several promising candidate assemblers and, for four of these (EWSR1, FUSQG, FUSN and TAF15N), we tested how their specificity changed when MCP was replaced with PCP and whether they exhibit nonspecific binding in absence of an RBD. Changing the RBD to PCP switched the RNA enrichment from mCherry:ms2 to EGFP::pp7, indicating that the recordanelle can be tuned by altering the RBD (Fig. 2c). Furthermore, in the absence of an RBD, we observed nonspecific RNA binding in the case of EWSR1 and FUSQG, which we suspect is because of these full-length proteins containing their own RBDs. However, recordanelles with the assemblers TAF15N or FUSN—comprising only IDRs without the C-terminal RBDs—appeared to lack this nonspecific binding activity. Together, this indicates that the recordanelle architecture components must be carefully selected and combined to balance enrichment efficiency and selectivity.To further characterize RNA recruitment efficiency and specificity, as well as assess the impact of recordanelle expression on the cellular transcriptome, we transiently transfected HEK293T cells with FUSQG-based recordanelle constructs that exhibited the highest selectivity and performed RNA-seq on full cells and the mitochondrial fraction (Fig. 2d). With MCP-based or PCP-based recordanelles, we did not observe any differentially expressed genes (DEGs) at the full cell level compared to ∆RBD; however, within the recordanelle fraction, the targeted RNA (that is, mCherry::ms2 or EGFP::pp7) was among the top (MCP) or the only (PCP) significantly enriched gene(s). For the MCP-containing recordanelle, we additionally observed one enriched predicted lncRNA and two depleted genes. While we attribute these subtle changes to technical noise, we cannot rule out that the enrichment of the lncRNA is caused by a so far undescribed binding to MCP.Importantly, we did not observe any alteration of the full cell transcriptome when comparing recordanelle-containing cells to a mock transfection control (Extended Data Fig. 2c), indicating that the expression of the recordanelle does not perturb the cell under these conditions. In sum, we show that recordanelles can be engineered to efficiently, specifically and tunably recruit specific target RNAs without disrupting the transcriptome.Capturing endogenous transcripts within recordanelles with poly(A) bindersWe next set out to extend the use of recordanelles from specific to generalized RNA recruitment by swapping the stem-loop-binding MCP/PCP RBDs for mRNA binders (Fig. 3a). Mammalian mRNAs are hallmarked by the 5′ cap and the poly(A) tail; therefore, we designed several different recordanelles with RBDs targeting these structures, including (1) human EIF4E to bind the 5′ cap28; (2) human LARP1, LARP4A, PABPN1, PABPC1 and PABPC4, yeast Pab1 and Nab2 and Escherichia coli Hfq and CspE to bind the poly(A) tail29,30,31,32,33,34; (3) catalytically deficient PARN28A,30A to bind the 5′ cap and the poly(A) tail35; (4) two versions of the mRNA nuclear export receptor Nfx1, containing only its RBDs or also the RRM, which are known to nonspecifically bind RNAs36; and (5) several versions of the poly(A)-binding protein PABPC4 (Supplementary Notes).Fig. 3: Capturing endogenous RNAs in recordanelles.Full size imagea, To recruit a broad spectrum of endogenous mRNAs in mammalian cells, a recordanelle is equipped with RBDs to either target the 5′ cap or the poly(A) tail. If such a recordanelle is expressed in cells together with mCherry::ms2 and EGFP::pp7 RNAs, both ectopically expressed genes and endogenous transcripts should be enriched in the mitochondrial fraction, while no RNAs are enriched without an RBD. b, A 3D reconstruction of cells expressing MA::TAF15N::PABPC4∆C (recordanelleV1), revealing faithful localization of the recordanelle to the mitochondrial surface. Hoechst, blue; mitochondrial marker, AIF, cyan; mCherry (protein), yellow; recordanelle (HA), magenta. Scale bar, 10 µm. (Supplementary Video 2). c, qPCR analysis of broad specificity RNA capture with several recordanelles in the mitochondrial fraction for cells cotransfected with the dual reporter and recordanelles containing the MA::TAF15N fused to various RBDs. Relative gene expression for mCherry, EGFP and YWHAZ was calculated using MT-ATP6 as the reference gene and mock transfection as the control sample. The heat map shows the mean of at least three independent experiments per condition (Extended Data Fig. 3c). d, Histogram of genes with respective log2FC in RNA-seq experiments of HEK293T cells expressing the dual reporter and a recordanelle with MA::TAF15N fused to the indicated RBD when compared to mock. The colored areas indicate the genes with FC above 1.5 and the corresponding percentage is the fraction of differentially enriched transcripts (FC of 1.5 and FDR of 0.01) in the recordanelle with the respective RBD over the total detected transcripts. e, Volcano plot of DEGs in the mitochondrial fraction and full cell RNA for the indicated recordanelles when compared to mock. Significantly upregulated or enriched genes are shown in magenta (|FC| of 1.5 and FDR of 0.01); downregulated or depleted genes are shown in blue. mCherry and EGFP are highlighted with stars.Just as we fixed the MCP/PCP RBDs when optimizing the assembler, we took the same approach here and fixed the assembler while varying the mRNA binders. To avoid any potential recordanelle saturation or nonspecific RNA binding from the FUSQG-based assembler, we initially used TAF15N as it exhibited moderate specific RNA enrichment and showed no nonspecific binding in previous assays without additional RBDs (Fig. 2c), providing a clean baseline for assessing the impact of the mRNA RBD on recordanelle performance.We first used IF to assess whether recordanelles faithfully localized to the mitochondrial membrane. While one recordanelle did not localize as anticipated (PABPN1), all others colocalized with a mitochondrial marker (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). We next tested for general RNA binding using mCherry, EGFP and YWHAZ recruitment within the mitochondrial fraction of dual-reporter-expressing HEK293T cells as a proxy (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). When comparing the recordanelles to control constructs lacking RBDs, we observed a range of recruitment behaviors. In several cases, the recordanelle constructs either weakly or did not enrich mRNA within the mitochondrial fraction and we did not characterize these further. However, the recordanelles based on LARP1/4A and variants of PABPC1/4 showed consistent and efficient mRNA recruitment within the mitochondrial fraction up to 15-fold.Encouraged by the generalized mRNA recruitment capacity of the recordanelles, we next tested combinations of top-performing assemblers (FUSQG, FUSN, EWSR1 and TAF15N) and RBDs (PABPC4∆C and PABPC4). Upon quantification of reporter and YWHAZ mRNAs within the mitochondrial and full cell fractions of transiently transfected HEK293T cells, we found that all recordanelle constructs could recruit mRNA within the mitochondrial fraction (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f). Moreover, this recruitment behavior was dependent on the RBD, indicating that recruitment was acting through generalized mRNA binding of the RBD rather than nonspecific binding because of the assembler. Whereas FUSQG was the most efficient at specific RNA recruitment when coupled with the stem-loop binders MCP and PCP, in these generalized mRNA recruitment experiments, TAF15N exhibited the highest binding of the reporter RNAs and the housekeeping RNA (YWHAZ). We speculate that this could be because of the RBD influencing the biomolecular condensation behavior of the assembler, which has been shown previously in the context of PABPC1 (ref. 37). This suggests that recordanelle performance depends on interactions between their component parts and, thus, combinatorial testing of recordanelle architectures could yield emergent properties.Transcriptome-wide recording with recordanellesTo deeply characterize recordanelle component combinations, we decided to go beyond using the reporter system and examine generalized mRNA recruitment on a larger unbiased scale with bulk RNA-seq. Specifically, we transiently transfected HEK293T cells with recordanelles based on combinations of top-performing assemblers (FUSQG and TAF15N) and RBDs (PABPC4∆C, PABPC4∆C161A, PABPC4 and LARP1) followed by RNA-seq on full cells and the recordanelle. As here we would expect to bind a substantial fraction of the transcriptome, we used synthetic RNA spike-ins to enable accurate global quantification of RNA enrichment38. When comparing each recordanelle to a mock transfection, we observed enrichment in a large portion of the transcriptome within the recordanelle, which was indicated by a positive shift in the log2 fold change (log2FC) density plots (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4). In the case of FUSQG-based recordanelles, some transcripts are enriched in the mitochondrial fraction in control constructs without an RBD, confirming the nonspecific RNA binding behavior of FUSQG observed previously (Fig. 2c), whereas RNA recruitment within TAF15N-based recordanelles was dependent on the presence of the mRNA binder.To quantify the global enrichment in RNAs within the recordanelle, we set a stringent threshold corresponding to an FC greater than 1.5 and a false discovery rate (FDR) less than 0.01, which revealed that 64% (FUSQG) and 90% (TAF15N) of genes expressed within HEK293T cells were enriched within the recordanelles compared to a nonbinding control. Importantly, this does not indicate that the recordanelles are bound to 64–90% of all RNA in the cell but, rather, that 64–90% of transcripts are represented in the recordanelles. In contrast, control constructs without an RBD showed an enrichment less than 0.1%. An analysis of DEGs further confirms transcriptome-scale enrichment of mRNAs within the recordanelle (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 4). Given that TAF15N-based recordanelles showed superior transcriptome-scale binding, we selected them as our lead constructs in subsequent experiments.This global enrichment occurs without altering the full cell transcriptome, likely because of only a small sampling of the cellular cytoplasmic pool being recruited to the recordanelle. In the presence of a PABPC4-containing or PABPC4∆C-containing recordanelle, we observe a high concordance between the whole cell and mitochondrial fraction (Extended Data Fig. 5), indicating that the enriched RNAs reflect the cytoplasmic RNA content of a cell. The few depleted or enriched transcripts within the mitochondrial fraction compared to the whole cell correspond to nuclear (for example, the lncRNA Xist) or mitochondrial RNAs, respectively, which can be expected from a recorder enriching cytoplasmic RNAs.Taken together, we have shown that several recordanelles architectures can capture a large fraction of the cytoplasmic transcriptome without altering global RNA levels in the cell.Recordanelles record transient gene expression eventsWe have thus far shown that recordanelles can recruit and accommodate a representative sampling of the transcriptome. We next aimed to assess whether the recordanelles could protect (that is, ‘record’) stored information throughout time. To test this, we developed a reporter cell line expressing mCherry::ms2 mRNA under a doxycycline (Dox) inducible promoter. In this cell line, when exposed to a transient Dox stimulus, mCherry::ms2 is robustly expressed but then returns to baseline levels after 1 day (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6). By quantifying the recovery of mCherry RNA from one day to the next, we can assess the capacity of recordanelles to protect RNAs throughout time.Fig. 4: Recordanelles efficiently record an engineered stimulus.Full size imagea, Illustration of reporter cell line containing Dox-inducible mCherry::ms2 in the genome. In a recording experiment, cells are exposed to Dox (50 ng ml−1) for 20 h before they are either harvested or the medium is exchanged to regular growth medium. Subsequently, they are harvested after 1 or 2 days. b, Bar graph of mean transcript recovery ratio ± s.d., defined for each replicate as the mCherry::ms2 mRNA level 1 day after removing Dox normalized to the corresponding mRNA level before removing Dox. Each cross represents one biological replicate. Relative mCherry::ms2 expression was obtained by qPCR analysis of reporter cell line transiently transfected with constructs encoding the indicated recordanelle and incubated with Dox (50 ng ml−1) for 20 h. Shown are the data for three biological replicates. c, Expression analysis by qPCR of mCherry::ms2 relative to MT-ATP6 for reporter cells transfected with the indicated recordanelle and exposed to Dox (50 ng ml−1, 20 h) (red) or not (gray). Left, bar graph showing samples collected right before Dox removal. Right, bar graph showing samples collected 2 days after removing Dox. Both full cell RNA and the RNA from the mitochondrial fraction were analyzed. Here, the data for mCherry::ms2 in the mitochondrial fraction are shown. Each dot represents one independent experiment (three biological replicates) and the line represents the mean. Relative expression is calculated compared to a control condition not exposed to Dox (Extended Data Fig. 6). Statistical significance was calculated using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparison test. NS, not significant; ****P ≤ 0.0001. Only in presence of a working recordanelle (recordanelleV1 (MA::TAF15N::PABPC4∆C) or recordanelleV2 (MA::TAF15N::PABPC4∆C161A)) can the transient presence of Dox be detected 2 days after its removal.To assess mCherry::ms2 protection by TAF15N-based recordanelles, we transfected the reporter cell line with recordanelle constructs followed by transient Dox treatment and mCherry qPCR at different time points. We then quantified the mCherry::ms2 mRNA ‘transcript recovery’ by comparing the ratio between values on days 1 and 0. A high ratio indicates that reporter mRNA levels are similar on days 0 and 1, indicating that the transiently expressed transcript was stabilized. Inversely, a low ratio signifies that most reporter transcripts have disappeared. Constructs containing PCP, MCP, LARP1 or LARP4A led to a transcript recovery at the full cell level of around 0.07, which was similar to the mock control, indicating that these recordanelles do not protect mCherry RNA (Fig. 4b). However, the PABPC1/4-based recordanelles led to 2–4-fold higher transcript recovery after 1 day. Even after 2 days, it was still possible to detect the mCherry transcripts in cells expressing the PABPC1/4-based recordanelles (Extended Data Fig. 6). This indicates that certain recordanelle architectures can both recruit and protect RNA for at least 48 h.One surprising result from this experiment was the fact that a subset of the recordanelles that we previously showed could recruit RNAs (LARP4A, LARP1 and MCP) did not protect mCherry::ms2 any better than a nonbinding PCP control. This was especially true for MCP-containing recordanelles that robustly bind mCherry::ms2. We speculate that this could be because of the ability of the RBD to protect the mRNA; for instance, whereas MCP binds before the poly(A) tail, PABPC4-based proteins directly bind the poly(A) tail and, thus, may shield the mRNAs against ribonucleases.To further characterize RNA protection within the TAF15N-based recordanelles containing either PABPC4∆C (recordanelleV1) or PABPC4∆C161A (recordanelleV2), we performed another mCherry::ms2 protection assay. This time, we harvested cells after 1 and 2 days and quantified mCherry::ms2 mRNA in both the whole cell and the recordanelle. In the control recordanelleMCP condition, we observed no difference in mCherry::ms2 between cells transiently treated with Dox and the untreated negative control after 2 days, at both the full cell and the recordanelle level. In contrast, in the recordanelleV1 and recordanelleV2 conditions, we observed significant mCherry::ms2 protection at the full cell (P = 0.0009 and 0.0106, respectively) and mitochondrial (P < 0.0001) levels (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6). These data confirm reporter RNA recording and protection, as well as indicate that, through recordanelle purification, we can substantially increase the sensitivity of detecting transient gene expression events. On day 0, when the reporter was maximally induced, mCherry::ms2 expression was higher in recordanelleV1 but not recordanelleV2 compared to the control recordanelleMCP (Extended Data Fig. 6). Because recordanelleV2 records this transiently expressed RNA without altering its initial expression level, it represents the superior architecture.Recordanelles enable the reconstruction of transient immune signalingHaving established that recordanelles can record ectopically expressed RNAs under Dox induction, we next wanted to explore whether they could also record more complex and dynamic endogenous gene expression events. For this purpose, we chose IFNB signaling as it has a defined transcriptional response in cells, leading to the upregulation of well-known IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs). We started by confirming that HEK293T cells exposed to increasing concentrations of IFNB show a dose-dependent increase in ISG overexpression (Supplementary Fig. 1).We then evaluated IFNB stimulus recording in cells expressing recordanelleV1 or recordanelleV2 (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 7). As a control, we expressed a recordanelle construct with the RBD MCP (recordanelleMCP), which should not bind mRNAs (as no ms2-tagged transcripts are present in this experiment). After 20 h of IFNB treatment in cells expressing recordanelles, for all conditions, we observed robust expression of the two representative ISGs—IFIT1 and IFI44L. We then removed IFNB and analyzed the ISG signal at the full cell and mitochondrial level 2 days later. Under control conditions, the ISG signal decayed completely and was indistinguishable from a control that had never been exposed to IFNB, whereas cells expressing recordanelleV1 or recordanelleV2 retained this information throughout time.Fig. 5: Recordanelles efficiently record endogenous immune signaling.Full size imagea, Illustration of experimental set up. HEK293T cells transiently expressing recordanelles are exposed to 60 U per ml of IFNB for 20 h before removal and cells are harvested directly or 2 days after IFNB removal. b, Expression analysis by qPCR of selected ISGs IFIT1 and IFI44L relative to MT-ATP6 in the mitochondrial fraction of cells expressing the indicated recordanelles. DEGs detected in recordanelleMCP + IFNB versus recordanelleMCP − IFNB (day 0, measure at the full cell level) (log2FC > 1, FDR 0.01) are considered ISGs under the experimental conditions and highlighted with purple dots in all volcano plots (Extended Data Fig. 7g and, for further controls, Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). d, Top ten Gene Ontology biological process (2025) terms for differentially upregulated genes in recordanelleV2 + IFNB versus recordanelleV2 − IFNB, day 2, ranked by FDR. For each term, the number of DEGs in the dataset is indicated relative to the total number of genes in that category. e, Correlation plot for recordanelleV2 + IFNB on both day 0 and day 2, showing the observed log2FC in the mitochondrial fraction and full cell RNA. The high correlation for ISGs indicates that the recordanelleV2 captures a representative fraction of the upregulated transcriptome. f, Full cell proteomics analysis of representative ISGs in presence of recordanelles. Experiment analogous to b. Proteomics analysis was performed on cells harvested 0 or 2 days after IFNB removal, the heat map shows the differential expression (calculated with an empirical Bayes moderated t-test with BH FDR correction using Proteoflux, |log2FC| > 1, FDR 0.01, three biological replicates) relative to a mock transfection not treated with IFNB (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Figs. 7–13). Significantly expressed proteins are indicated by a star, protein expression levels not passing within-contrast filtering conditions (Methods) are colored in gray and fully imputed proteins in one arm (without an applicable FC) are shown in black with a white triangle. g, UMAP embedding of single-cell RNA-seq experiment analogous to b, showing ten distinct clusters in cells expressing recordanelleMCP or recordanelleV2, transiently treated with IFNB and analyzed 0 or 2 days after removing IFNB (Extended Data Fig. 10a). h, Dot plot of cells corresponding to g for the expression of top ten marker genes in cluster 6. Dot size indicates the percentage of expressing cells; color of the heat map indicates the mean expression. Top marker genes of cluster 6 are ISGs and we term this cluster the IRC. i, Difference of cluster representation for recordanelleMCP/recordanelleV2-expressing cells, either never treated with IFNB (top) or transiently treated with IFNB (bottom), 2 days after transient IFNB treatment. The IRC is only present in transiently stimulated recordanelleV2-expressing cells. j, On the basis of the ISGs defined previously (Extended Data Fig. 7g and Extended Data Fig. 10b), we define an ISG expression module and, here, we plot the ISG expression for recordanelleMCP-transfected cells 0 or 2 days after IFNB removal. k, Analogous to j, we show the ISG expression module for recordanelleV2-transfected cells.Under certain conditions we observed that, in recordanelleV1-containing cells, ISG detection was not only maintained but increased from day 0 to 2 after IFNB removal (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 7a,b); this could occur under conditions where the recorded ISG mRNAs are translated. This increase appeared specific to IFNB signaling as it was absent for the YWHAZ housekeeping gene. As we did not observe this behavior for recordanelleV2, it seems that this version is superior as an RNA recording tool and we, therefore, proceeded with this recordanelle architecture.To probe the limits of recording with recordanelleV2, we next characterized its behavior over an extended period of time (Extended Data Fig. 7c–f, Supplementary Fig. 2 and 3). In nonpassaged cells, the IFNB signal is lost in recordanelleMCP controls after 2 days, whereas, for recordanelleV2-expressing cells, we still efficiently recorded ISGs after 5 days (Extended Data Fig. 7c,e). In passaged cells, recordanelles capture ISGs 3–4 days after stimulus removal but the signal is lost from day 5 onward. The recordanelle operates by enriching and protecting endogenous RNAs in a synthetic organelle mounted on the surface of mitochondria. This is achieved with a single fusion protein containing a mitochondrial anchor, assembler peptide and RBD. Our optimized recordanelles capture a subset of all mRNAs—reflecting up to 90% of the transcriptome—over multiple days and cell divisions, enabling transient and complex transcriptional events to be archived within single cells. Recordanelles achieve this without substantially altering cellular viability or mitochondrial function, as well as the cellular transcriptome and proteome under the conditions tested in this study. The degree of the apparent recording seems to be influenced by the cellular state, such that, without passaging, we can record IFNB signaling for at least 5 days, whereas the signal decays more quickly with passaging. We interpret this as proliferation increasing the turnover of the transcriptional record, whereby previously recorded transcripts can be lost and newly transcribed mRNAs are recorded in their place.While the data reported here suggest that recordanelles do not substantially perturb cellular function under the tested conditions, it is important to clarify that transcriptional recorders such as recordanelles by their very nature are perturbations to cells. These perturbations include the burden of transgene expression, occupancy of the mitochondrial membrane and its immediate surroundings, unnatural interactions with the RNAs they track, depletion of RNAs from the cellular pool and thermodynamic costs of information storage. As the field moves from building technologies to applying them to ask fundamental questions about biology, exactly how these perturbations manifest and potentially confound our interpretation of biology remains to be seen.Molecular recording technologies have emerged to solve fundamental challenges in observing, tracking and measuring biological systems throughout time. Whereas prior strategies rely on encoding information by modifying DNA, RNA or protein, our approach differs in that it functions by continuously storing unmodified biological molecules within a protective intracellular compartment that is straightforward to extract and sequence independent. Recordanelles are scalable, unbiased, fast, continuous and tunable and can record the whole transcriptome with single-cell sensitivity. Additionally, they only require the expression of a single protein of approximately 91 kDa (2.5 kb), which is small enough to be efficiently transfected or delivered with common viral vectors such as lentiviruses or adeno-associated viruses.
